title: Steel Water Tank Base: Sand Pad, Ring Beam or Concrete Slab?
excerpt: Which base does your steel water tank need? A plain guide to sand pads, concrete ring beams and slabs, with the pros, cons and best uses of each.
content:
The base under a steel water tank decides how long the tank lasts. A good base keeps the liner flat, the bottom of the wall dry and the tank level for decades. A poor base lets the edge wash away, the floor sink and the wall rust at ground level.

There are three main options for a steel water tank base: a compacted sand or crusher-dust pad, a concrete ring beam, or a full concrete slab. This guide explains each one in plain language, with the pros and cons, and helps you choose the right one for your tank and your ground.

Quick answer: which water tank base do I need?

  • Small tank (up to about 6 m wide) on firm, level ground: a compacted sand or crusher-dust pad is usually enough.
  • Bigger tank (about 6 m wide and up), a tank with a roof in a windy spot, a sloping site or sandy ground: use a concrete ring beam.
  • Problem ground (dolomite or clay that swells), drinking water or fire water, or a tank close to a house: use a concrete slab designed for the site.

Not sure? Send us a few photos of the site and we will tell you which base fits.

Why the base matters so much

Most of our corrugated steel tanks have no steel floor. A strong PVC liner holds the water. It lies on a protective floor sheet on top of the base and runs up the inside of the steel wall.

That means the base is the floor of your tank. Everything under the liner must be smooth, firm and level.

The weight itself is not the big problem. A full tank 2.3 m high presses down with about 2.3 tonnes on every square metre, and most firm, compacted ground can carry that. What really damages a tank is:

  • A soft edge that sinks or spreads under the wall.
  • A floor that sinks in the middle or tilts, which stretches the liner and pulls the wall out of round.
  • Rain or overflow washing the base away at the edge.
  • Soil, water or plants against the bottom of the wall, which makes the steel rust there first.
  • Stones or sharp edges under the liner, which can puncture it.

A good base solves all five.

Option 1: compacted sand or crusher-dust pad

This is a flat, level platform of compacted sand, crusher dust or fine gravel, built a bit wider than the tank. Geotextile (a tough fabric) stops the fill mixing with the soil and protects the liner. The liner's floor sheet goes straight on top.

Good points

  • Cheapest and quickest. It can be ready in a day or two with a plate compactor and farm labour.
  • Soft on the liner. The fine surface is kind to the PVC.
  • Drains well. Water does not stand under the floor.
  • Easy to fix or move. You can re-level it or move the tank later.

Weak points

  • The edge is the weak spot. Rain and overflow wash the edge away, and the sand spreads out under the wall over time.
  • Nothing to bolt to. An empty tank, especially one with a roof, can be moved by strong wind.
  • Only as good as the ground under it. On soft or problem ground it will sink unevenly.
  • Needs looking after. You have to keep the edge topped up and protected.

Tip: hold the edge in with a ring of blocks or a steel edge, and put a band of stones around the tank so roof water cannot wash the pad away. It costs little and fixes the biggest weakness.

Best for: small and medium tanks on firm, flat ground in a sheltered spot.

Option 2: concrete ring beam

A ring beam is a reinforced concrete ring that sits under the tank wall, like a kerb in a circle. The inside of the ring is filled with compacted sand or crusher dust, and the liner lies on that.

Think of it as the best of both worlds. The concrete ring gives the steel wall a solid, level seat. The sand inside still gives the liner a soft, free-draining bed.

Good points

  • The wall stays level. The ring gives a firm, accurate base to build the tank on.
  • The edge cannot wash away. The ring holds the fill in place.
  • Stops the edge sinking. The wall load sits on concrete, not loose sand.
  • Something to bolt to. The tank can be anchored against wind.
  • Keeps the bottom of the wall dry and up off the soil.
  • Still kind to the liner, because the floor is sand, not concrete.

Weak points

  • Costs more and takes longer. You need digging, steel, shuttering, concrete and about a week to cure.
  • It must be built accurately. If the ring is not level or round, the tank will not be either.
  • Does not fix bad ground in the middle. The fill inside can still sink if the soil under it is soft.
  • The joint needs care. The joint between the wall and the concrete must be sealed and must shed water.

Best for: tanks from about 6 m wide and up, tanks with a roof in windy areas, sloping sites and sandy or coastal ground. For most larger farm tanks, this is the base we recommend.

How big should a ring beam be?

That depends on the tank size, the wall height and your soil, so there is no one size for all tanks. Large oil tanks overseas use rings at least about 300 mm wide, but a lined water tank puts much less weight on its wall, so the right size can differ. Your ring beam should be sized by an engineer for your tank and site. Damtech can advise on this when we quote your tank.

Option 3: full concrete slab

A reinforced concrete slab is cast over the whole footprint of the tank, usually a little wider. The wall stands on the slab, and the liner goes on a protective underlay on top.

Good points

  • The strongest and most even base. It will not wash away, rut or sink at the edge if it is designed properly.
  • You can see leaks. If the liner ever leaks, the water runs out at the edge where you can see it, instead of soaking into the ground. On some ground that is very important (see below).
  • Anchors can go anywhere.
  • Lowest maintenance over the life of the tank.

Weak points

  • The most expensive option, and it needs a week or more to cure before the tank goes up.
  • Must be smooth. A rough slab can wear through a liner, so it needs a smooth finish and a protective underlay.
  • Thin slabs crack. The thin slabs used under small plastic tanks are not strong enough for a big steel tank. It must be designed for the full weight of water.
  • Cannot be moved.

Best for: problem ground, drinking-water and fire-water tanks, and tanks close to houses, roads or slopes where a leak would cause damage.

Sand pad vs ring beam vs concrete slab: side by side

Sand or crusher-dust pad Concrete ring beam Concrete slab
Cost Lowest Medium Highest
Time to build 1 to 2 days About a week, with curing A week or more, with curing
Kind to the liner Yes Yes Only with a smooth finish and underlay
Edge washes away? Can do No No
Tank stays level Fair Good Best
Can anchor against wind No Yes Yes
Leaks visible No, they soak away No, they soak away Yes, if detailed for it
Problem ground Not suitable Limited Best starting point
Can be moved later Yes No No
Best for Small tanks, good ground Larger tanks, wind, slopes, sand Problem ground, drinking or fire water

Your ground matters more than your tank size

In South Africa, the soil under the tank can change the answer completely. Check these before you choose a base.

Dolomite land (parts of Gauteng, including Centurion)

About a quarter of Gauteng sits on dolomite. Here, leaking water is the main cause of sinkholes. A water tank is a big source of water in one spot, so a leak into a sand pad on dolomite is exactly what you must avoid.

If your property is on dolomite land, find out its dolomite rating first (your municipality or a geotechnical report will have it), and get an engineer's advice. In most cases a concrete slab with a planned leak path, and rainwater led well away, is the safer base.

Clay that swells (black or "turf" clay)

Some clays swell when they get wet and shrink when they dry. A leaking or overflowing tank wets the soil on one side only, so the ground lifts unevenly and the tank goes out of level. On this ground, the clay is usually dug out and replaced, or a stiffened slab is used, with a concrete apron that sends water away from the tank.

Sandy, coastal and windy sites

Loose sand washes and blows away easily, so an open sand pad is not ideal. Use a ring beam, or at least a pad with a firm edge. On windy coastal sites, anchoring a roofed tank is worth it, and sea air means the steel and concrete at ground level need extra care.

Sloping sites

Do not build up loose fill on the low side to make a flat pad. It will settle and wash away. Cut a level platform into firm ground, and use a ring beam to hold the edge.

Galvanised or Aluzinc tank on concrete? Read this first

The steel at the bottom of the wall needs protecting on any base.

  • Galvanised (Z275) steel is fine on fully cured concrete, but should not be set into wet, fresh concrete.
  • Aluzinc steel should never touch concrete, even old concrete, if it can get wet. The alkaline concrete attacks the aluminium in the coating.
  • On a ring beam or slab, put a bitumen separator strip under the wall and seal the joint so water runs off it.
  • On every base, keep soil, stones, grass and weeds off the bottom of the wall. Wet dirt against steel is where rust starts.

Learn more in Aluzinc vs galvanised steel water tanks.

Water tank base checklist

Whichever base you choose, check these before the tank arrives:

  1. Clear the site. Remove topsoil, roots and plants.
  2. Compact the ground in layers. Never build on loose fill.
  3. Make it level. Check it across the full width in several directions.
  4. Make it wider than the tank, so the edge is not right at the wall.
  5. Finish with a smooth, fine layer with no stones or sharp bits.
  6. Protect the edge with a ring, blocks or a stone band.
  7. Slope the ground away from the tank so rain runs off.
  8. Pipe the overflow and drain well away from the base.
  9. Keep the bottom of the wall clear of soil and plants. Our guide to vegetation management around reservoirs explains why.

Frequently asked questions

Can I put a steel water tank straight on the ground?

No. Bare soil sinks unevenly, holds water against the steel and can have stones that puncture the liner. Always build at least a level, compacted sand or crusher-dust pad.

Is a ring beam better than a concrete slab?

For most larger farm tanks on normal ground, yes. A ring beam is cheaper than a slab, keeps a soft sand bed under the liner and still gives a solid, level seat for the wall. A slab is better on problem ground or where leaks must never reach the soil.

Is sand or crusher dust better for a tank base?

Both work when compacted properly. Crusher dust packs firmer and washes away less. Use a fine grade with no sharp stones, and put geotextile between it and the liner.

Do I need an engineer for my tank base?

For a small tank on good ground, usually not. For a large tank, a ring beam, a slab, or any site on dolomite, swelling clay, fill or a slope, yes. The base must be designed for your tank and your soil.

Is the base included in the tank price?

No. Damtech's tank kit prices exclude the base, delivery and installation. We can quote base work and installation separately.

How long does a base take before the tank can go up?

A sand or crusher-dust pad can be ready in a day or two. A concrete ring beam or slab needs about a week or more to cure first.

Get the right base for your tank

title: Climate Resilience and Water Security: Strategic Water Storage Infrastructure for South Africa's El Niño Summer
excerpt: El Niño 2026/27 makes on-farm storage the most controllable water investment. How to size, specify and site tanks and reservoirs that outlast the drought.
content:
South Africa is entering a very strong El Niño. NOAA declared El Niño conditions in June 2026 and put the odds of a "very strong" event at about 63%. On 1 September the South African Weather Service (SAWS) said Pacific sea-surface temperatures had already crossed the very-strong threshold.

The most likely outcome is a hotter, drier summer over most of the country, with more frequent heatwaves. For farms, lodges and businesses, the question is practical: what water storage infrastructure will still be working when the dry spell bites, and still be sound when the next one comes?

This guide is about that infrastructure. It covers how much storage to plan for, which storage type suits which job, and how material choices decide whether a drought-year purchase is a lasting asset or a repeat cost. For the climate background, read El Niño 2026/27: what it means for water security on South African farms.

Why on-farm storage is the investment you control

National bulk storage looks strong. National dam storage was about 95.6% on 2 November 2026, against about 55% in August 2016. The Integrated Vaal River System was around 98 to 100%.

But full national dams protect irrigators and cities, not every farm. Three weak points matter for storage planning:

  1. Rain-fed land and small dams. About 80% of field crops are rain-fed. Boreholes and small earth dams respond quickly to dry spells and high evaporation.
  2. Groundwater is not guaranteed. In the 2015/16 drought, 29 of 89 emergency boreholes came up dry.
  3. The Western Cape is the exception. After one of its driest winters in decades, provincial storage was about 78.5% on 2 November 2026. Voëlvlei was at 59% and Steenbras Lower at 47% in early September, both full a year earlier. Cape Town has entered a drought-caution phase, and agricultural allocations from the Berg and Breede systems are at risk if the next winter is also dry.

Damtech's El Niño research concludes that on-farm water storage, rainwater harvesting and leak repair are the most direct, controllable investments farmers can make before the peak of the season. The Department of Agriculture's advisory also calls for more water and feed points for livestock.

For businesses, the risk is different. DWS has said recent municipal outages were caused by leaks, ageing pumps and insufficient storage and pumping capacity, not drought. National non-revenue water is about 47.3%, worth about R26 billion a year. Gauteng and eThekwini are seen as most exposed to summer outages. Backup storage is the buffer between an outage and a stopped operation.

Plan for Scenario B, test against Scenario C

The research sets out three scenarios for the season. Scenario B, a 2023/24-type season with a damaging mid-summer dry spell, is a reasonable planning base. Scenario C, a 2015/16-type drought, is the stress test.

Scenario Rainfall Water outlook
A. Mild (1997/98-type) Near-normal in parts of the summer region Bulk supply secure; municipal outages from leaks
B. Moderate (2023/24-type) Damaging dry spell and heat in January to February Bulk secure; Western Cape restrictions likely if next winter is dry
C. Severe (2015/16-type) Persistent below-normal rain, repeated heatwaves Pressure on bulk systems by late 2027, especially the Western Cape

For storage, that means sizing to ride through a dry spell of several weeks in January and February, then checking what happens if it runs into a second dry year.

Step 1: Size storage to the gap, not the tank catalogue

Storage size is an engineering calculation, not a guess. Work it out from four numbers:

  1. Daily demand in litres: people, livestock, irrigation, processing or cleaning. Use your own meter or pump records where you have them.
  2. Reliable daily supply: what the borehole, municipal connection or rainfall actually delivers on a bad day, not a good one.
  3. Days of autonomy: how many days you need to bridge a borehole failure, a pump repair, load-shedding or a municipal outage.
  4. A margin for heat. Hot weather raises demand from stock, people and crops, and raises evaporation from open water.

Required storage ≈ (daily demand − reliable daily supply) × days of autonomy, plus margin.

Damtech's water storage calculators do this arithmetic for tanks and dams. For a quick comparison of tank sizes, see the steel water storage tanks range, from 10 000 L kits to reservoirs of 500 kL and more.

One rule of thumb from the 2015/16 drought: do not assume the borehole will carry the shortfall. Size storage so a borehole failure is an inconvenience, not a crisis.

Step 2: Choose the right storage type for the job

Storage type Best suited to Watch out for
Lined earth dam (HDPE or PVC) Large irrigation and stock volumes where land is available Evaporation from a large open surface; liner quality and installation
Corrugated steel reservoir with liner Borehole buffering, stock water, lodge and estate supply, fire reserve, sites where a dam is not practical Base preparation, coating choice for the site, liner thickness
Steel tank on a stand or plinth Gravity feed, rooftop or yard backup for businesses Concrete contact and coating compatibility
Rainwater harvesting tank Capturing summer storms; supplementing other supply Soft, slightly acidic water; first-flush diversion

Lined dams carry the largest volumes at the lowest cost per litre. If your existing dam leaks, fix that first: see how to drought-proof your farm dam before El Niño peaks. For dams, the liner decision is covered in our HDPE dam lining and PVC dam lining guides.

Steel reservoirs go up fast, need no excavation and can be placed where the water is used. For livestock-specific layouts, read livestock water in a drought year.

Step 3: Specify materials that outlast the drought

A tank bought in a hurry and specified loosely can fail inside five years. That turns an emergency purchase into a repeat cost, often during the next dry cycle. Capital security in a drought year comes from three decisions, in this order: the water barrier, the base, then the coating.

The water barrier comes first

Damtech's coating research found that neither thin galvanised sheet nor Aluzinc should be relied on bare as the long-term water barrier.

  • Z275 galvanised sheet carries only about 19.3 µm of zinc per face. In soft water, industry rates would consume it in about 2 to 4 years if sustained.
  • Aluzinc has no fresh-water immersion rate in anything found.

So the inside of a drought-resilience tank needs a qualified liner or a heavier system such as batch galvanising or a certified factory coating. Damtech's Z275 galvanised and AZ150 Aluzinc corrugated tanks are supplied with a 550 gsm PVC liner, with 850 gsm on request.

This matters most where drought storage is fed by soft water:

  • Rainwater is low in the salts that protect zinc. Highveld rain has been measured at pH 4.65 to 4.80.
  • Western Cape municipal water is soft. Cape Town supply reported for January to March 2026 had hardness of 16 to 46 mg/L as CaCO₃, below the 50 mg/L line where zinc is prone to severe attack.

The Western Cape is the region with the weakest El Niño buffer and the softest water. Line every tank there.

The base comes second

  • Build on a level, compacted base of sand or crusher dust on geotextile, so settlement does not stress the liner.
  • Keep Aluzinc off concrete. Alkaline concrete attacks the aluminium, even when cured. Use a separator membrane, a sealed joint and drainage.
  • Keep soil, vegetation and debris off the wall base. Our post on vegetation management around reservoirs covers this.

The coating comes third

Choose the exterior coating for the site's atmosphere:

  • Inland farms, C2 to C3: lined Z275 galvanised or Aluzinc tanks both give long exterior life.
  • Coastal sites within about 1 km of the sea: the first 150 m is classed CX and 150 to 1,000 m is mid-C4 to mid-C5 (Janse van Rensburg et al., 2019). Bare Z275 gives a planning line of about 4 years in C5, against about 14 years for AZ150 Aluzinc. Use AZ200 with an organic coat and sealed edges, or a duplex system.

The full evidence is in galvanised vs Aluzinc steel water tanks.

Fittings and water quality

  • Keep copper out of and upstream of galvanised tanks. About 0.1 ppm of dissolved copper can cause rapid pitting of zinc.
  • Fit first-flush diversion on rainwater systems and discard the first fill.
  • Cover stored water. El Niño summers still bring storms and flash floods that can contaminate open supplies, and the research notes that intermittent municipal supply pushes households toward unsuitable containers, raising disease risk.
  • For drinking water, check against SANS 241: zinc has an aesthetic limit of 5 mg/L.

Step 4: Order early

Storage takes time to make and deliver. Damtech's published lead time for supply-only tank kits is 5 to 10 business days to manufacture after cleared payment, plus 3 to 5 business days for delivery: about 8 to 15 business days in total. Base preparation and installation add to that.

SAWS's guidance is that a conservative management strategy is advisable in El Niño summers. The critical maize window is late January to February, and heatwaves raise livestock water demand sharply. Storage ordered in December may not be ready when it is needed most.

Step 5: Keep it working through the season

  • Inspect weekly in hot weather: liner condition, fittings, float valves and overflow.
  • Fix leaks immediately. A small leak in a full reservoir is a large loss over a dry month. Our leak repair guide for corrugated steel reservoirs explains the common causes.
  • Monitor SAWS outlooks monthly and DWS reservoir reports weekly. The research recommends watching rainfall and heat during January to February and Western Cape winter rainfall from April to July 2027.

Key takeaways

  • National dams are full, but farms on boreholes, small dams and rain-fed land are exposed, and so is the Western Cape.
  • Size storage to the supply gap, assuming the borehole may fail.
  • Specify the liner first, then the base, then the coating.
  • Line every tank on soft or rain water, and use coastal-grade exteriors near the sea.
  • Order early: kits take about 8 to 15 business days before installation.

Send us your water source, daily demand, site and the outage or dry spell you need to cover. We will size the storage, specify the liner, base and coating, and quote it.

title: Livestock Water in a Drought Year: Steel Tanks, Troughs and Reservoirs
excerpt: Secure livestock water before El Niño peaks. How steel tanks, troughs and reservoirs protect your herd when boreholes and dams come under pressure.
content:
Livestock farming is usually the sector hit hardest in an El Niño drought, because grazing, drinking water and animal condition all decline together. With a very strong El Niño forecast for the 2026/27 summer, a reliable supply of livestock water is the first thing to secure. This guide covers how steel water tanks, troughs and reservoirs can protect your herd when borehole and dam supplies come under pressure.

For the wider forecast, see our guide to El Niño and farm water security in South Africa.

Why livestock are so exposed in a drought year

The 2015/16 El Niño drought shows the scale of the risk. Around 186,000 livestock died and nearly 247,000 farmers were affected, with the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Mpumalanga hardest hit. Researchers warned that the loss of breeding stock would cause shortages for two to four years afterwards (Scholtz et al., 2016).

This season the pressure is layered. The foot-and-mouth disease outbreak, declared a national disaster in early 2026, limits movement and slaughter, so farmers cannot always destock quickly when grazing runs out. The Department of Agriculture's advice is to keep herd sizes in line with veld carrying capacity, practise rotational grazing, keep feed reserves and increase the number of water and feed points (Department of Agriculture advisory).

What heat does to livestock water demand

Above-normal temperatures are very likely this summer, and heat stress cuts feed intake, fertility, conception rates, milk yield and weaning weights. Animals also drink more when it is hot, so livestock water points are one of the weakest links during a heatwave. A trough that is fine in a normal summer can run dry quickly when demand climbs and the source is a borehole or dam under pressure.

Why borehole and dam supply is not enough on its own

  • Boreholes can fail. Of 89 emergency boreholes drilled in 2015/16, 29 were dry.
  • Small earth dams draw down fast in hot, windy weather, and the remaining water warms and deteriorates. See our guide to farm dam water quality for livestock.
  • Power and pump problems can cut supply even when the source is full. Our article on water storage tips for borehole shortages explains how storage covers the gap.

Storage you control is the answer. A tank or reservoir filled steadily from your borehole or dam gives you days of buffer, so a pump failure or dry spell does not immediately become an animal welfare problem.

Choosing storage for livestock water

Corrugated steel water tanks

Corrugated steel tanks suit farm storage because they come in a range of capacities and are assembled on site. Our steel water storage tanks range includes sizes such as the 10,000 litre, 20,000 litre, 50,000 litre and 100,000 litre tanks, so you can match capacity to herd size and refill rate.

Livestock troughs

A steel livestock water trough gives animals clean access to water and keeps them out of the dam, which protects both water quality and the dam wall. Adding troughs in more camps spreads grazing pressure and follows the advice to increase the number of water points.

Reservoirs and lined dams

For larger operations, a reservoir or a properly lined dam holds the volume needed for big herds. Read our cost-benefit analysis of corrugated steel reservoirs and our agricultural water storage page for how dams, tanks and troughs work together.

How much storage do I need?

The right volume depends on your herd size, the daily demand in hot weather, how reliably your source refills the tank, and how many days of buffer you want. Use our water storage calculators to put numbers on it, and ask us to review your figures if you are unsure.

Keep your storage working through the season

  • Check tank floats, valves, pipelines and troughs before the heat arrives.
  • Look for leaks. Corrugated steel reservoirs can develop them over time, and our guide to leak repair for corrugated steel reservoirs shows how to spot early signs.
  • Follow a maintenance routine. See how to extend the life of corrugated steel reservoirs.
  • Keep stocking rates in line with water and grazing, and plan to sell older or unproductive animals early while prices are reasonable.

Frequently asked questions

How can I make sure my livestock have water during a drought?

Add storage you control, such as tanks and troughs, fed from your borehole or dam, and increase the number of water points so animals are not concentrated at one source.

What size water tank do I need for cattle?

It depends on herd size, hot-weather demand and how quickly your source refills the tank. A calculator and a site assessment give a far better answer than a rule of thumb.

Are steel water tanks good for farm use?

Corrugated steel tanks are widely used on farms because they come in a range of capacities and can be assembled on site. Look at the capacity options and request a quote for your herd and layout.

title: How to Drought-Proof Your Farm Dam Before the El Niño Summer Peaks
excerpt: Check your farm dam for seepage and leaks, repair or line it, and add backup storage before the El Niño summer. A practical South African checklist.
content:
A very strong El Niño is forecast to bring a hotter, drier summer to much of South Africa. If your farm relies on an earth dam, now is the time to check it. The water you capture in good years is only useful if it is still there when the dry spell arrives. This guide covers how to drought-proof a farm dam before the El Niño summer peaks.

For the wider forecast picture, read our overview of El Niño and water security on South African farms.

Why your dam needs attention this summer

National dam levels are high, at about 95.6% in early November 2026 according to the Department of Water and Sanitation. That protects big irrigation schemes and municipal supply, but it does not top up your private dam. A hotter summer raises both evaporation and water demand, so a farm dam draws down faster than usual. SAWS advises a conservative management approach in El Niño summers, and for a dam owner that starts with knowing how much water you are losing.

The two silent losses: seepage and evaporation

Seepage

Seepage is water that escapes through the floor and walls of the dam. Sandy soils lose water quickly, while clay can crack as it dries. A dam that holds less than it should is also one that gives you less reserve when it matters. Our guide to dam lining for sandy and clay soils explains how soil type affects losses.

Evaporation

Evaporation is the loss from the water surface, and it rises in hot, dry, windy weather. You cannot stop it entirely, but you can limit the damage by fixing seepage and pipe leaks first, so that evaporation is the only major loss left, and by keeping water in fewer, deeper storage points rather than several shallow ones. Our water-saving tips for farm dams cover more of these options.

Step 1: Check whether your dam is leaking

Start with a simple test: compare how fast the water level falls with how fast it should fall from evaporation alone. If the level drops faster, you probably have a leak. Walk the crest and toe of the embankment looking for wet patches, soft ground, erosion or green growth that stays lush in dry weather. For a full checklist, see our farm dam leak diagnosis and repair guide.

Also check the pipes, valves and outlets. They are often the real source when a dam seems to lose water overnight.

Step 2: Repair what is failing before it widens

Small leaks and torn liner sections tend to grow under UV exposure, stock traffic and wind. Repairing early is cheaper than relining later. If you already have a liner, look for:

  • Tears or punctures near the waterline, where sun and wind do the most damage
  • Seams that have lifted or failed
  • Liner pulling away from the crest or anchor trench
  • Damage around inlet and outlet pipes

Our leaking dam repair service covers failed geomembrane liners and water storage systems. You can also read how to prevent costly farm dam liner failures.

Step 3: Line the dam if it loses too much water

If an unlined dam will not hold water, or an old liner is beyond patching, lining is the long-term fix. The common options are:

  • HDPE dam lining, a tough geomembrane suited to large earth dams and reservoirs
  • PVC dam lining, a flexible option for ponds and smaller farm dams
  • Torch-on lining, bitumen membranes for cement dams and canals

Our farm dam linings page explains which option suits livestock water and irrigation storage, and our dam lining cost guide covers what drives the price. If you are in Limpopo or Mpumalanga, two of the more exposed regions, see our local pages for Limpopo dam liners and Mpumalanga dam liners.

Step 4: Protect water quality as levels fall

As a dam drops, the remaining water warms, concentrates and tends to grow algae. That matters most when animals drink from it. Keep stock out of the dam where you can, and use troughs fed from the dam instead. Our guide to farm dam water quality for livestock explains what to look for.

Step 5: Add backup storage you control

Do not rely on one dam. In 2015/16, 29 of the 89 emergency boreholes drilled came up dry, so groundwater is not a guaranteed backup. A tank or reservoir next to your dam or borehole gives you a buffer for pumping outages and dry spells. See our corrugated steel water storage tanks, and read how to integrate borehole water with farm dams.

To work out how much you need, use our dam lining and water storage calculators.

El Niño dam checklist

  1. Compare your dam's level drop against expected evaporation.
  2. Walk the embankment and look for wet patches and erosion.
  3. Inspect any liner for tears, lifted seams and damaged pipe connections.
  4. Repair or reline before the hottest months.
  5. Check pumps, valves, pipelines and troughs.
  6. Add tank storage next to your dam or borehole.
  7. Keep stock numbers in line with your water supply.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if my farm dam is leaking?

If the water level falls faster than evaporation can explain, or you see wet ground at the toe of the embankment, you likely have a leak. A site inspection can confirm where it is coming from.

Can a lined dam still lose water?

Yes. Tears, failed seams and damaged pipe connections can all let water out of a lined dam, which is why regular inspection matters.

Is it worth lining a dam before a drought?

If your dam loses significant water to seepage, lining it before the dry season means more of the water you capture stays available. A quote based on your dam's dimensions will show the cost against the benefit.

title: Galvanised Z275 Steel Water Tanks in South Africa: What the Zinc Coating Can and Cannot Do
excerpt: A practical engineering guide to galvanised steel water tanks in South Africa: what Z275 means, how zinc protects steel, and where it falls short.
content:
Galvanised steel water tanks are the most common steel storage option on South African farms, lodges and industrial sites. Most buyers see "galvanised" and assume decades of rust-free service. The truth is more useful than that. A galvanised coating does excellent work in the right conditions and fails quickly in the wrong ones.

This guide explains what a Z275 galvanised coating actually is, how zinc protects steel, and how it behaves in South African water. It covers hard borehole water, soft Western Cape supply, acidic rainwater and coastal air. It also explains why the liner, not the zinc, usually decides how long a tank lasts.

What "Z275" means on a galvanised steel water tank

The "Z" grades describe continuously galvanised steel sheet. Steel coil runs through a molten zinc bath at the mill and comes out with a thin zinc layer on both faces. The number is the total coating mass on both faces, in grams per square metre.

That detail matters. Z275, the grade Damtech uses for its galvanised tanks, does not mean 275 g/m² on each side. It means roughly 137.5 g/m² of zinc per face, which works out to about 19.3 µm per face at nominal thickness. The lighter Z250 grade, common in the market, gives about 17.5 µm.

Grade Total coating, both faces (g/m²) Nominal thickness per face (µm) Zinc per face (g/m²)
Z275 275 19.3 137.5
Z250 250 17.5 125

Figures derived from coating mass and the density of zinc (7.14 g/cm³), as set out in GalvInfoNote 1.1.

Two further points catch buyers out:

  • One face is usually thinner. Coating mass is measured as an average across both faces. For Z275, the thinner face is around 13 to 14 µm (GalvInfoNote 1.1). Inside a tank, that thinner face may be the one holding water.
  • Grades vary by standard. Z275 appears in EN 10346 grade lists, while Z250 is missing from at least one of them. Whatever you buy, ask for the mill certificate and check the standard and designation it states.

Sheet, not plate, and not batch galvanising

Z275 is a coil-coated sheet product, normally in light gauges. It is not structural plate. It is also different from batch hot-dip galvanising, where a finished, fabricated item is dipped after forming.

Batch galvanising builds zinc-iron alloy layers usually 55 to over 100 µm thick (HDGASA Info Sheet 6). That is roughly three to five times the zinc on one face of Z275. Batch work falls under SANS 121 / ISO 1461. ISO 1461:2022 expressly excludes continuously galvanised sheet, so a "SANS 121 compliant" claim on a Z275 sheet tank is the wrong reference.

This is why long-life stories about old pressed-steel tanks do not transfer to thin sheet. Those tanks were usually batch galvanised with far more zinc.

How zinc protects a steel water tank

Zinc protects steel in two ways.

  1. Sacrificial (cathodic) protection. Zinc is more reactive than steel. Where the coating is scratched or cut, the zinc corrodes first and protects the exposed steel nearby.
  2. A protective surface film. In the right water, zinc forms a carbonate-based film that slows further corrosion. Hardness and alkalinity in the water support this film.

The second mechanism is the important one inside a tank. Zinc's corrosion rate in water depends heavily on water chemistry. In hard, scale-forming water the film can almost stop corrosion. In soft, low-alkalinity water the film struggles to form, and zinc is consumed much faster.

Continuous immersion vs fluctuating water levels

Fully submerged walls

Industry tables give typical zinc loss rates for fresh water. The table below shows how long one wetted face of Z275 would last if those rates were sustained.

Water type Typical zinc loss (µm/year) Z275 face, 19.3 µm (years) Batch galvanised, 85 µm (years)
Hard fresh water 2.5–5 3.9–7.7 17–34
Soft fresh water 5–10 1.9–3.9 8.5–17

Rates from the GAA/GANZ durability guide. Years are simple division and indicate scale only.

Read this table as an order of magnitude, not a service-life promise. Two effects pull in opposite directions. Scale can slow zinc far below these rates in hard water. But pits, cut edges and the thinner face fail ahead of the average.

The message is still clear. About 19 µm of zinc is a thin reserve for a wetted surface.

The waterline band

Many farm tanks cycle between full and half-full. That creates a band of wall that is wet, then dry, then wet again.

The evidence here is thin. In seawater, zinc in tidal and splash zones typically corrodes about twice as fast as fully immersed zinc (HDGASA Info Sheet 3). The American Galvanizers Association adds that agitation accelerates waterline attack in fresh and sea water (AGA).

No fresh-water waterline test or tank teardown was found. A static waterline with sediment or biofilm is a likely weak point, but that is an engineering inference, not a measurement.

The headspace under the roof

The air gap above the water is humid and poorly ventilated. On zinc, trapped moisture produces loose white rust (GalvInfoNote 3.3). Condensate is also soft water, even when the stored water is hard. No tank-headspace study was found, so treat the roof underside as a wet, not an atmospheric, surface.

Galvanised tanks and South African water

South Africa's water varies sharply by source and region. That variation matters more for a galvanised tank than the coating grade does.

South African water What it does to zinc Practical reading
Soft, low-alkalinity supply Zinc is prone to severe attack below 50 mg/L as CaCO₃ (HDGASA) Worst realistic case. Line the tank
Hard, scale-forming borehole water Scale can virtually stop corrosion at pH 6 to 8 Zinc's best case
Chlorinated municipal water Chlorine at drinking levels is not a proven driver Low alkalinity is the real risk
Rainwater Highveld rain measured at pH 4.65 to 4.80, below zinc's stated lower limit of about pH 5.5 to 6 Line the tank

The Western Cape is a soft-water region. Every City of Cape Town supply reported for January to March 2026 fell below the 50 mg/L line. Hardness ranged from 16 to 46 mg/L and alkalinity from 8 to 26 mg/L as CaCO₃ (City of Cape Town). Bare zinc in that water is in its least favourable class.

Rainwater harvesting tanks face the same problem. Rain lacks the dissolved salts that build zinc's protective film. Highveld rain readings come from Water SA. Contact with roof dust and the tank itself will raise the pH in storage somewhat, but not enough to rely on.

Hard borehole water can be zinc's friend. If a laboratory analysis shows scale-forming chemistry, bare zinc has a documented protective mechanism. Get the analysis before relying on it. Hardness, alkalinity, pH, chloride, sulphate and copper are the minimum.

Copper deserves a special warning. About 0.1 ppm of dissolved copper is named as enough to cause rapid pitting of zinc (GAA). Keep copper pipe and fittings out of, and upstream of, a galvanised tank.

Positives and engineering advantages of galvanised Z275

  • More sacrificial zinc than Aluzinc at a similar thickness. Z275 carries about 4.2 times the zinc per face of AZ150 Aluzinc. Zinc is the metal that does the sacrificial work. See Aluzinc water storage tanks for the detail.
  • A documented mechanism in water. Zinc is the only one of the two coatings with a described self-protecting film in fresh water, provided the water is hard and scale-forming.
  • Better short-term cut-edge behaviour. Cleveland-Cliffs, which sells both products, says galvanised may show less cut-edge red rust than aluminium-zinc in the short term, under about 10 years depending on environment (product data).
  • Tolerates cured concrete. Galvanising embedded in sound concrete is reported to corrode below 0.1 µm/year. That makes zinc the more forgiving coating where a tank bears on a cured, separated plinth.
  • Forms well. Zinc coatings adhere well through tight bends and corrugations, which suits roll-formed tank sheets.
  • Familiar repairs. Zinc-rich repair systems are established and widely available.

Negatives and environmental limitations

Coastal and industrial air (ISO 9223 C3 to C5)

The outside face of a tank lives in the atmosphere. Corrosivity is classed from C1 (very low) to CX (extreme). Using ISO 9224 long-term zinc rates, a Z275 face at nominal thickness gives these planning lines:

Atmosphere Z275 planning line (years) Published Z275 range (years)
C3 (medium, most inland and many coastal-hinterland sites) about 18 12–42
C4 (high) about 9 5–12
C5 (very high) about 4 2–5

Planning lines are derived from the top of the ISO 9224 steady-state zinc rates. The ranges are published for Z275 in the GAA/GANZ guide. Multiply by about 0.7 for the thinner face.

South Africa's peer-reviewed corrosion map shows how fast the class rises near the sea. The first 150 m from the shore is CX, and 150 to 1,000 m sits in mid-C4 to mid-C5 (Janse van Rensburg et al., 2019). Sites 1 to 30 km inland are largely C3. Those classes were measured on steel, so a site's zinc class should be checked, not assumed.

For a tank within a kilometre of the sea, bare Z275 on the outside is a short-life coating. Paint, duplex systems or a different coating are worth pricing.

Soft water, acidic water and the inside face

As above, soft water and rainwater are zinc's worst cases. A bare Z275 tank in Cape Town supply or on a rainwater system should be treated as a consumable, not a long-term asset.

Drinking water

SANS 241-1:2015 sets an aesthetic limit for zinc of 5 mg/L. Australian guidance reports legacy galvanised rainwater tanks typically at 2 to 4 mg/L zinc, and up to 11 mg/L (NHMRC). No potable-water certification for a bare galvanised sheet surface was found. For drinking water, specify a wetted surface with its own evidence.

Specifications and the DWS 9900 benchmark

The Department of Water and Sanitation's DWS 9900 corrosion protection specification is written mainly for pipelines and galvanised articles. It does not name Z275 or tank sheet, and it binds only where a contract invokes it. Its galvanising chapter still sets the benchmark a reviewing engineer is likely to use:

  • Heavy-duty galvanising starts at 55 µm for steel below 1.5 mm. Z275's 19.3 µm per face is about 35% of that.
  • Galvanised structures are not to be subjected to stagnant water, on oxygen-depletion grounds.
  • A water analysis goes to the corrosion engineer, who decides whether an internal polymer lining or overcoat is needed.

So DWS 9900 does not ban galvanised steel in water. It does expect a lining decision based on the water.

International bolted tanks are covered by ANSI/AWWA D103, which addresses factory-coated bolted steel tanks. A light-gauge corrugated farm tank is a different product class.

Where a galvanised steel water tank makes sense

The research points to one clear rule. Specify the water barrier first and the metallic coating second.

  • Lined galvanised tank. The liner carries the water duty, and the zinc protects the shell from the outside air and from incidental moisture. This is the configuration Damtech supplies: its corrugated galvanised tanks come with a 550 gsm PVC liner (850 gsm on request) and a bidim floor sheet, over a Z275 galvanised shell. Damtech also supplies AZ150 Aluzinc tanks with the same liner.
  • Unlined galvanised tank in hard water. Defensible only with a water analysis showing scale-forming chemistry, the heaviest available coating, and an owner who accepts a finite life with inspections.
  • Unlined galvanised tank in soft or acidic water. Not recommended. Line it.

For long-life unlined steel, the stronger route is batch galvanising at heavy-duty thickness or a certified factory coating, not thin sheet.

What galvanised steel water tanks cost in South Africa

There is no reliable published price bracket for Z275 tanks across the South African market. Prices depend on diameter, height, sheet gauge, coating grade (Z275 galvanised or Aluzinc), liner, roof, fittings, transport and installation. Commercial and industrial tanks are priced to a specification.

For reference, Damtech's current supply-only kit prices, including VAT, PVC liner and standard fittings, are:

Damtech kit Size (diameter × height) Price incl. VAT
10 000 L water tank 3 m × 1.5 m R13 999
20 000 L water tank 4 m × 1.5 m R18 999
50 000 L water tank 5 m × 2.3 m R31 999
100 000 L water tank 9 m × 1.5 m R43 999

Delivery, base preparation and installation are excluded and quoted separately. Larger reservoirs, from about 11 kL to 500 kL and beyond, are quoted per project on the steel water storage tanks page.

When comparing quotes, ask each supplier for the coating grade per face, the mill certificate, the liner thickness and what is excluded. A cheaper tank with a thinner coating and no liner is not a like-for-like price.

Key takeaways

  • Z275 means about 19.3 µm of zinc per face, not 275 g/m² per side.
  • Zinc protects well in hard, scale-forming water and poorly in soft, acidic or rain water.
  • On the outside, bare Z275 is a short-life coating within about 1 km of the coast.
  • A qualified liner is what makes a galvanised steel water tank last.

For the full side-by-side picture, read Aluzinc vs galvanised steel water tanks. If you are buying storage ahead of a dry summer, see El Niño 2026/27 and water security on South African farms.

title: Aluzinc Water Storage Tanks: Engineering Performance and Longevity
excerpt: Aluzinc is excellent on the outside of a tank and unproven under water. An engineer's guide to how the coating works and where it belongs.
content:
Aluzinc has a strong reputation in South Africa. Roofing suppliers sell it on long life in coastal air, and some tank sellers claim it outlasts galvanised steel many times over. One South African seller advertises a seven-fold advantage without citing a test.

The reputation is real, but it was earned on the outside of buildings, not under water. This guide explains how the coating works, where it clearly outperforms zinc, and where the evidence runs out. If you are choosing an Aluzinc water tank, this is the difference that decides whether it lasts. Damtech supplies both AZ150 Aluzinc and Z275 galvanised tanks, each with a 550 gsm PVC liner, so this guide is about fitting the coating to the site, not selling one over the other.

What Aluzinc is

Aluzinc is a trade name for steel sheet with a 55% aluminium-zinc alloy coating. The same class of product is sold as Zincalume and Galvalume. Engineers often write it as "Al-Zn" or "AZ", followed by the coating mass, such as AZ150.

Like galvanised "Z" grades, the number is the total coating mass on both faces in g/m². AZ150 is not 150 g/m² per side.

One supply check matters before anything else. BlueScope's current Zincalume data sheet describes an aluminium-zinc-magnesium alloy alongside AZ labels. A magnesium-bearing grade is a different coating from classic 55% Al-Zn. Confirm the alloy on the mill certificate.

The microscopic layer structure

Under a microscope, Aluzinc is a two-phase composite (GalvInfoNote 1.4):

  1. Aluminium-rich dendrites. These tree-like crystals make up most of the coating volume. They act as a barrier, because aluminium forms a tough oxide film.
  2. A zinc-rich interdendritic network. Zinc fills the spaces between the dendrites as a connected labyrinth. This is the part that does sacrificial (galvanic) work, corroding to protect exposed steel.
  3. A thin intermetallic layer. This bonds the coating to the steel base. It is hard and brittle.

By simple rule of mixtures, the coating is about 75% aluminium by volume. The often-quoted 80% figure could not be traced to a primary source.

Thicker than galvanised, with far less zinc

Aluminium is much lighter than zinc. So for the same coating mass, Aluzinc is thicker. But it holds much less zinc.

Coating Nominal thickness per face (µm) Zinc per face (g/m²) Zinc compared with Z275
Z275 galvanised 19.3 137.5 100%
AZ150 20.0 32.6 about 24%
AZ185 24.7 40.2 about 29%
AZ200 26.7 43.5 about 32%

Derived from published equivalence of AZ150 with about 20 µm per face, and 43.5% zinc by weight (GalvInfoNote 1.4).

AZ150 is about as thick as Z275, slightly thicker in fact, but holds only about a quarter of its zinc. That single fact explains most of what follows.

How Aluzinc protects steel: barrier plus galvanic action

In the open air, Aluzinc's behaviour is excellent. The zinc-rich network corrodes first. Its corrosion products then plug the labyrinth, and the loss curve flattens instead of running in a straight line. The aluminium-rich dendrites carry on as a barrier.

That is why long atmospheric programmes show Aluzinc lasting about two to four times as long as galvanised steel of equal thickness. Townsend's 25-year data found it about three times galvanised in severe marine exposure and still intact.

Exterior life by atmosphere

Applying a factor of three to ISO 9224 zinc rates gives these planning lines for one face at nominal thickness:

Coating C3 (years) C4 (years) C5 (years)
Z275 (for comparison) about 18 about 9 about 4
AZ150 54 27 14
AZ185 67 34 17
AZ200 73 36 18

Derived planning lines. No standard publishes Al-Zn rates by corrosivity category, so these columns are constructed, not measured. Multiply by about 0.7 for the thinner face: AZ150 becomes roughly 38, 19 and 10 years.

The exterior advantage is about 3.1 times for AZ150 over Z275, once Aluzinc's slightly greater thickness is included. Against the lighter Z250 grade it is about 3.4 times. Values above about 30 years are arithmetic rather than experience, because the longest exposure records found run to about 30 years.

Warranties near the sea sit well below this arithmetic. BlueScope's next-generation roofing terms run up to 10 years at 100 to 200 m from severe marine influence, rising with distance. Those terms cover a magnesium-bearing roofing grade, not a tank, but they show how fast coastal exposure shortens what a producer will stand behind. That is a useful reality check for coastal sites such as the Overstrand.

Cut edges and scratches: how much "self-healing" is real?

"Self-healing" is a common sales phrase for Aluzinc. It oversells what has been measured for either coating.

What the evidence does show:

  • Chloride helps Aluzinc's edges. In chloride, both phases activate and the steel stays protected. In sulphate solution, protection lasted only for short immersion times (Vu et al., Corrosion Science 2011).
  • Marine and industrial air are its strong suit. A five-year study found both coatings giving good cut-edge protection in marine and industrial air, lasting longer on Aluzinc, and little protection in rural and urban air (Palma and Morcillo).
  • Drying matters. A producer study found corrosion products adhering at cut edges only when a drying step was included (Matsumoto et al.).
  • Thickness limits it. A common rule of thumb is that Aluzinc cannot protect a cut edge on steel thicker than about 1 to 2 mm. The test basis for that rule was not found.

No immersed cut-edge or bolt-hole measurement in fresh water was found for either coating. In high-humidity air near the coast, Aluzinc's edge holds up well over the long term. Inside a fresh-water tank, the indirect evidence suggests its edge protection is weaker. Seal cut edges and bolt holes on any wetted face rather than relying on galvanic action.

Aluzinc under water: the evidence gap

This is the most important section for anyone buying an Aluzinc water tank.

No fresh-water immersion corrosion rate for 55% Al-Zn was found from any source. That is a statement about what the research found, not proof that none exists. But it means nobody can honestly quote an under-water lifespan for bare Aluzinc.

What exists points both ways:

  • For Aluzinc: in seawater and salt solutions it generally outperforms galvanised steel. In 0.5 mol/L salt solution, its cathodic protection lasted 260 hours against 153 hours for zinc (study record). Aluminium metal also resists neutral soft water well.
  • Against relying on it: the same seawater work reports serious pitting in the fully immersed zone (Springer record). Fresh water lacks the chloride that activates Aluzinc's edge protection. And only about a quarter of the zinc is available to act sacrificially.

Producers are cautious too. BlueScope's TB-3 recommends its polymer-laminated product, on a zinc substrate, for water tanks, and says of the strainer that Zincalume "must not be continually immersed". That sentence concerns one component, and BlueScope sells the alternative, so weigh it with care. Cleveland-Cliffs warrants its Al-Zn sheet only under normal atmospheric exposure and excludes constant fresh-water spray.

The fair summary: Aluzinc in fresh-water immersion is unknown, not shown to be poor. Until coupon tests in real South African waters exist, a bare Aluzinc wall should not be the water barrier.

Positives of Aluzinc water storage tanks

  • Outstanding exterior durability. About 3.1 times the planning life of Z275 on a freely exposed, draining outer face.
  • Better in coastal air. Chloride activates its edge protection, and its marine cut-edge performance lasts longer than zinc's over the long term.
  • Better in seawater and salt solutions overall, with a pitting caveat.
  • A clean outer skin on a lined tank. Market practice already pairs it this way: one South African maker combines AZ150 with a multilayer PVC liner. That is consistent with the liner carrying the water duty.

Negatives and limitations

  • Alkaline conditions attack the aluminium. U.S. Steel warns of alkali attack on both coatings above pH 9 (U.S. Steel). South African drinking water limits allow pH up to 9.7.
  • Concrete plinths need isolation. GalvInfo advises no contact between Aluzinc and concrete, including cured concrete that may get wet (GalvInfo). Use a separator membrane, a sealed joint and drainage at the base. Flush water that has stood on fresh concrete.
  • Brittle on tight bends. The intermetallic layer cracks more readily in heavier coatings. U.S. Steel favours the lighter coating for tight bends, which limits the gain from moving up to AZ200 on corrugated profiles.
  • Thin-sheet only. It is a coil product. It cannot be applied after fabrication, so structural plate and thick panels go to batch galvanising or paint.
  • Closed headspace. Trapped moisture causes dark storage staining. Its effect on coating life inside a tank roof is unmeasured.
  • Drinking water. No NSF/ANSI 61 or AS/NZS 4020 listing for a bare 55% Al-Zn surface was found. SANS 241 sets an operational limit of 300 µg/L for aluminium.
  • Specifications. DWS 9900 does not name Aluzinc. Its galvanising chapter limits zinc-bath impurities to 1.5%, so a 55% aluminium bath is not "galvanising" under that chapter. No public evidence was found that AWWA D103 recognises Al-Zn, though its text was not read. On a contract invoking DWS 9900, an Aluzinc tank needs approval as an unnamed system.

Where an Aluzinc water tank fits

Situation Recommended Avoid
Lined light-gauge tank, C2 to C3 site AZ150 shell with a qualified liner Quoting exterior life as tank life
Lined tank, C4 site AZ185 or AZ200, checked on the real profile for cracking Assuming a heavier grade always helps
Coastal C5, about 150 to 1,000 m from the sea AZ200 with an organic coat and sealed edges, or a duplex system Treating bare Aluzinc as maintenance-free
Within about 150 m of the sea Move the tank if possible, or use a full coated system Bare sheet of any kind
Concrete base Separator membrane, sealed joint, drainage Bare Aluzinc on concrete
Unlined tank in fresh water Only after coupon evidence in that water Lifetime claims from atmospheric data

What Aluzinc water tanks cost

No sourced South African price data for Aluzinc tanks or sheet was found, so no ZAR figures are given here. The main cost drivers are the same as for any steel tank: coating grade, sheet gauge, diameter and height, liner, roof, fittings, freight and installation. On coastal sites, edge sealing and an organic overcoat add cost but also add life.

When comparing an Aluzinc quote with a galvanised one, compare like with like: the same liner, the same coating mass per face, and the same exclusions. For a side-by-side on lifecycle value, see Aluzinc vs galvanised steel water tanks.

Key takeaways

  • Aluzinc is about 75% aluminium by volume and holds only about a quarter of Z275's zinc.
  • It is the better coating on the outside of a tank, by about 3.1 times over Z275 on planning lines.
  • No fresh-water immersion rate was found. A liner should carry the water duty.
  • Keep it off concrete and away from alkaline water.

For the zinc side of the story, read galvanised Z275 steel water tanks in South Africa.

Talk to an engineer before you specify

The right tank depends on your site's distance from the sea, your water source and your base. Send us your location, water analysis if you have one, and storage target, and we will recommend the coating, liner and base to suit.

title: Galvanised vs Aluzinc Steel Water Tanks: What Really Protects the Water
excerpt: Aluzinc wins on the outside of a tank and zinc has the only documented mechanism under water. The comparison that matters is which face of the tank a claim describes.
content:
Ask ten suppliers whether Aluzinc or galvanised steel makes the better water tank and you will hear ten confident answers. Most of them compare the wrong thing.

A steel water tank has two very different faces. The outside lives in the air. The inside lives in water. The famous Aluzinc advantage was measured on the outside. Under water, the evidence looks almost reversed, and for Aluzinc it is largely missing.

This comparison sets galvanised Z275, the grade Damtech uses, against 55% aluminium-zinc (AZ150 to AZ200) for South African tanks. Damtech supplies both. It separates what is measured from what is derived, and it ends with a practical rule for specifying a tank that lasts.

The short answer

  • On the outside, Aluzinc is the stronger coating, by about 3.1 times over Z275 on planning lines.
  • On the inside, neither bare coating should be relied on as the long-term water barrier. Zinc has a documented protective mechanism only in hard, scale-forming water. Aluzinc has no fresh-water immersion rate in anything found.
  • So specify the water barrier first: a qualified liner, or a heavier system such as batch galvanising, duplex or a certified factory coating. Then choose the metallic coating for the outside.

Head-to-head comparison table

Read the table by row and by evidence. Rows for the outside face cannot be transferred to the inside face.

Criterion Galvanised Z275 Aluzinc (55% Al-Zn, AZ150) Advantage Evidence strength
Coating composition Near-pure zinc, single layer About 75% aluminium by volume; Al-rich dendrites with a zinc-rich network — Secondary sources
Thickness per face, nominal 19.3 µm 20.0 µm About equal Derived from coating mass
Zinc per face 137.5 g/m² 32.6 g/m² (about 24% of Z275) Galvanised Derived
Exterior loss rate, C3 0.4–1.1 µm/year 0.10–0.55 µm/year Aluzinc Zinc from ISO 9224; Al-Zn derived
Exterior loss rate, C4 1.1–2.2 µm/year 0.28–1.10 µm/year Aluzinc As above
Exterior loss rate, C5 2.2–4.4 µm/year 0.55–2.20 µm/year Aluzinc As above
Exterior planning life, C3 / C4 / C5 about 18 / 9 / 4 years (published Z275 ranges 12–42 / 5–12 / 2–5) 54 / 27 / 14 years Aluzinc, about 3.1 times Derived planning lines

Exterior rates: zinc from ISO 9224 bands reproduced in the GAA/GANZ guide. Aluzinc columns are derived by dividing zinc rates by a life multiple of 2 to 4 (GalvInfoNote 1.4); no standard publishes Al-Zn rates by category. Planning line = µm per face ÷ top of the steady-state band (÷ 3 for Al-Zn).

Why the outside and inside give opposite answers

Outside: Aluzinc's labyrinth plugs itself

In the open air, Aluzinc's zinc-rich network corrodes first. The corrosion products plug the network, and the aluminium-rich dendrites keep acting as a barrier. The loss curve flattens. That is the mechanism behind its well-earned roofing reputation.

Galvanised zinc corrodes by roughly uniform thinning. With about 19.3 µm per face on Z275, it runs out sooner.

Inside: zinc has a film, Aluzinc has a question mark

Under water, zinc depends on a carbonate film that hardness and alkalinity support. In hard, scale-forming water it can nearly stop corrosion. In soft water the film struggles.

Aluzinc's plugging mechanism was observed in air. Nothing found shows it working the same way under continuous immersion. In low-chloride water, the working anode is largely the zinc-rich network, which holds only about a quarter of Z275's zinc at AZ150. That is reasoning from laboratory salts, not a fresh-water measurement.

Producers lean cautious. BlueScope's TB-3 recommends a polymer-laminated product on a zinc substrate for water tanks. Cleveland-Cliffs excludes constant fresh-water spray from its Al-Zn warranty.

Water chemistry: which tank suits your water?

Your water Galvanised Z275 Aluzinc Recommendation
Hard borehole water, scale-forming Best case; documented film No scale benefit shown Zinc may suit better, but test first
Soft municipal, e.g. Cape Town Worst case below 50 mg/L CaCO₃ Unknown Line the tank
Rainwater Below zinc's pH range on the Highveld Unknown Line the tank; first-flush diversion
Chlorinated municipal Residual not a proven driver Not studied Watch alkalinity, not chlorine
Water above pH 9 or standing on new concrete Tolerant Alkali attacks aluminium Galvanised, or isolate Aluzinc

Cape Town supply reported for January to March 2026 had hardness of 16 to 46 mg/L and alkalinity of 8 to 26 mg/L as CaCO₃ (City of Cape Town). Every supply fell below the line where zinc is prone to severe attack. Highveld rain has been measured at pH 4.65 to 4.80 (Water SA).

Coastal sites: where Aluzinc earns its premium

South Africa's corrosion map puts the first 150 m from the shore in CX and 150 to 1,000 m in mid-C4 to mid-C5 (Janse van Rensburg et al., 2019). For a coastal property or farm, the outside of the tank faces the harshest conditions.

On producer rates for severe marine sites, Z275 lasts about 2 years and AZ150 about 9 years before the face is consumed. For marine sites further back, the figures are about 15 years for Z275 and 37 years for AZ150. Those rates come from a BlueScope technical guide seen only as an extract, so treat them as indicative.

Practical rule for coastal tanks: AZ200 with an organic coat and sealed edges, or batch galvanising with a duplex paint system, both over a liner. Measure the site class rather than assuming it.

El Niño 2026/27: why material choice matters this season

South Africa is heading into a very strong El Niño. The South African Weather Service favours below-normal rainfall over most of the country for October 2026 to January 2027, with more frequent heatwaves. Storage bought in a hurry is exactly where coating choices get rushed.

Three findings from Damtech's El Niño research connect directly to tank specification:

  1. The Western Cape enters summer after a very dry winter. Provincial dam storage was about 78.5% on 2 November 2026, against a national figure of about 95.6%. That region also has soft water and long coastlines: the two conditions where bare zinc performs worst.
  2. Boreholes are not a guaranteed fallback. In the 2015/16 drought, 29 of 89 emergency boreholes came up dry. Rainwater harvesting and stored municipal water fill the gap, and both are soft. A tank bought for drought resilience must be lined.
  3. Municipal outages come from leaks and pumping, not empty dams. National non-revenue water is about 47.3%. DWS sees Gauteng and eThekwini as most exposed to summer outages. If backup storage stands on a concrete slab or plinth, an Aluzinc tank must be isolated from the concrete.

A tank that fails in five years turns an emergency purchase into a repeat cost, often in the next dry cycle. Capital security in a drought year comes from the liner and the base, then the coating. For the wider planning picture, see El Niño 2026/27 and water security on South African farms.

Lifecycle cost-effectiveness

There is no sourced ZAR price comparison between Z275 and Aluzinc tanks, so this section reasons from life rather than price.

  • Lined tank, inland site (C2 to C3): both coatings can give long exterior life. Z275 is adequate for many farm sites; Aluzinc adds margin. The liner sets the replacement interval.
  • Lined tank, coastal site (C4 to C5): Aluzinc's exterior life advantage is worth paying for, provided the base is isolated and edges are sealed.
  • Unlined tank: neither bare sheet coating is a long-life design. Batch galvanising at 55 to 85 µm gives about three to four times Z275's zinc per face and is the better long-life route where metal must touch water.
  • Concrete plinth: galvanised is the more forgiving coating; Aluzinc needs a separator membrane.

Damtech's current kit prices for lined Z275 corrugated galvanised tanks are listed on the steel water storage tanks page. AZ150 Aluzinc tanks, with the same PVC liner, are quoted on request.

How to specify your tank

  1. Get a water analysis: hardness, alkalinity, pH, chloride, sulphate and copper.
  2. Classify the site: distance from the sea and from heavy industry.
  3. Choose the water barrier: a qualified liner of stated thickness, or a batch-galvanised or factory-coated wetted surface.
  4. Choose the exterior coating for the site class.
  5. State the coating per face and require the mill certificate.
  6. Seal cut edges and bolt holes, isolate dissimilar metals, and keep copper out of the system.
  7. Design the base: level and compacted, with a separator where steel meets concrete, and dirt and vegetation kept off the wall base.

For the detail on each coating, read galvanised Z275 steel water tanks and Aluzinc water storage tanks.

Standards referenced

  • DWS 9900, Department of Water and Sanitation General Corrosion Protection Specification, second edition, July 2022. It names neither coating and applies by contract.
  • ANSI/AWWA D103-19, factory-coated bolted carbon steel tanks. Its clause text was not reviewed for this article.
  • ISO 9223, atmospheric corrosivity categories. It does not describe tank interiors.
  • ISO 1461 / SANS 121, batch galvanising. It excludes continuously galvanised sheet.
  • SANS 241-1:2015, drinking water: zinc 5 mg/L (aesthetic), aluminium 300 µg/L (operational).

Get an engineered tank specification

Damtech specifies and supplies lined Z275 galvanised and Aluzinc steel reservoirs for farms, lodges, estates and industrial sites across South Africa. Tell us your water source, site and storage target, and we will recommend a size, liner, coating approach and base, and quote it.

Request a reservoir specification and quote or use our water storage calculators.

This article is general technical information, not a design or compliance opinion for a specific project. Aluzinc atmospheric rates are derived, not measured, and no figure here is a warranty.

title: El Niño 2026/27: What It Means for Water Security on South African Farms
excerpt: A very strong El Niño is under way. See what SAWS forecasts, where South African farms are most exposed and how to secure farm water before summer peaks.
content:
South Africa is heading into one of the strongest El Niño events on record, and the water risk it brings is very different from one farm to the next. National dams are close to full, yet many farms still depend on a single borehole, a small earth dam or a few tanks. This guide pulls together the latest forecasts and what they mean for water security on South African farms in the 2026/27 season.

Forecasts describe probabilities, not certainties, so treat this as a planning guide and check the latest outlooks from the South African Weather Service (SAWS) as the season unfolds.

What is El Niño, and how strong is this one?

El Niño is a warming of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean that shifts weather patterns around the world. Over southern Africa it tends to bring lower summer rainfall and higher temperatures, although the effect varies from season to season.

NOAA's Climate Prediction Center issued an El Niño Advisory in June 2026 and put the chance of a "very strong" event at about 63%. On 1 September SAWS said Pacific sea-surface temperatures had already crossed the very-strong threshold and that the event could become the strongest in living memory, peaking between about October 2026 and January 2027 (SAnews).

What the forecasts say for South African farmers

  • Below-normal rainfall is favoured over most of the country for October to December 2026, and November to January looks very similar.
  • Above-normal temperatures are considered very likely, with heatwaves more frequent if the dry conditions materialise.
  • The far north-east, including the Kruger National Park area, is expected to be hardest hit, and KwaZulu-Natal can expect El Niño effects from October 2026 to March 2027.
  • The event is not expected to fade until around February or March 2027, close to the end of the summer cropping season.

SAWS has also cautioned that a strong El Niño does not automatically mean severe drought. Of the three very strong events since 1979, 1982/83 and 2015/16 brought widespread drought, but 1997/98 brought slightly above-normal rain to parts of the summer rainfall region. Its advice is simple: manage conservatively and prepare early.

Why full dams do not mean every farm is safe

South Africa enters the season in a much stronger position than in 2015. National dam storage was about 95.6% on 2 November 2026, compared with about 55% in August 2016, according to the Department of Water and Sanitation's weekly reservoir report. Soil moisture and veld are also in good condition after a long, wet 2025/26 season.

That protects bulk supply and irrigation schemes, but it leaves real gaps:

  • About 80% of field crops are rain-fed. Full dams do little for dryland maize or grazing when summer rain fails.
  • The Western Cape had one of its driest winters in decades. Its main supply system was around 79% in September, with several key dams far below last year, and agricultural allocations are at risk if the next winter is also dry.
  • Boreholes and small farm dams react fast. In 2015/16, 29 of 89 emergency boreholes drilled came up dry, which shows that groundwater is not an automatic fallback in a deep drought.
  • Municipal systems lose a large share of water to leaks. National non-revenue water is about 47%, so outages can happen even when dams are full.

In other words, the most useful question for a farmer is not "are the dams full?" but "how much water do I have stored, and how much of it will I lose before I use it?"

Where farm water is most exposed this summer

RegionMain water exposure
Limpopo and MpumalangaRain-fed crops, cattle, communal grazing and heat stress on subtropical fruit
Free State and North WestDryland maize and sunflower; livestock grazing. Dams are full, but rain-fed land is exposed
KwaZulu-NatalSugarcane, veld-fire risk and municipal water losses
Eastern CapeLivestock, which suffered heavy losses in 2015/16
Western CapeLow dam levels after a dry winter and possible allocation cuts

These ratings are a qualitative summary of the research, not an official classification.

Lessons from the 2015/16 drought

The last very strong El Niño left a clear record. About 246,600 farmers were affected and roughly 186,000 livestock died. Researchers warned that the loss of breeding stock would cause livestock shortages for two to four years afterwards (Scholtz et al., 2016). Relief arrived late: by March 2016 only about 42,000 farmers had been assisted (SAnews).

The practical lesson is that the farms that coped best were those that had secured water and feed before the dry spell hit.

Practical steps to secure farm water now

  1. Find and fix leaks. A dam or reservoir that loses water through seepage or a failed liner is losing your drought reserve. Our guide to diagnosing farm dam leaks shows what to look for, and our dam repair service can assess a leaking dam on site.
  2. Line unlined or failing dams. Dam linings such as HDPE reduce seepage losses so more of the water you capture stays available.
  3. Add storage you control. Tanks and reservoirs next to your borehole or dam give you a buffer. See our corrugated steel water storage tanks and our agricultural water storage solutions.
  4. Add water points for livestock. The Department of Agriculture advises increasing the number of water and feed points, so check your troughs, pumps and pipelines before the heat arrives.
  5. Plan your levels. Our guide on managing farm dam water levels during prolonged droughts covers how to stretch what you have.
  6. Size your storage properly. Use our water storage calculators to estimate lining area and tank size before you ask for a quote.

What to watch over the coming months

  • Monthly: the SAWS seasonal outlook and NOAA's ENSO update.
  • Weekly: DWS reservoir reports for your catchment, plus your own dam and borehole levels.
  • Late January to February 2027: rainfall and heat during maize flowering, the most critical yield window.

Frequently asked questions

Will El Niño cause a drought in South Africa in 2026/27?

Below-normal rainfall is favoured, but it is not guaranteed. Impacts will depend on local rainfall and other climate drivers. Because a very strong El Niño has brought both severe drought and near-normal rain in the past, preparing for a dry summer is the safer plan.

Are South African dams full going into El Niño?

Nationally, yes: storage was about 95.6% in early November 2026. The Western Cape is lower, at around 79%, and farms that rely on boreholes, rainfall or small private dams are not protected by national dam levels.

What is the best way for a farmer to prepare for El Niño?

Secure and protect your own water: repair leaks, line dams that lose water, add storage and water points, and match livestock numbers to your grazing and water supply.
